articles.title: I Gave a Monkey 10 Million Keystrokes a Day on My GitHub Profile (It's Trying to Write Hamlet)
articles.excerpt: Give a monkey a typewriter and infinite time, and it will eventually type the works of Shakespeare. That's the infinite monkey theorem. I got bored of a normal GitHub profile README. So I put the theo…
articles.body: Give a monkey a typewriter and infinite time, and it will eventually type the works of Shakespeare. That's the infinite monkey theorem . I got bored of a normal GitHub profile README. So I put the theorem on mine. Every day a GitHub Action hands my pixel monkey 10,000,000 random keystrokes and checks whether any of them landed on Hamlet. The stats update on the README. The longest match so far is "o the bla" — nine characters, somewhere in Act IV. At this pace, finishing the play takes about 10^237421 years. Cool.
articles.author: Marcel Losso Forte

articles.title: Implement File Export with Temporary Download Links Using Presigned URLs
articles.excerpt: Implement File Export with Temporary Download Links Using Presigned URLs Short answer: keep the exported file private, generate a presigned download link only after the export completes, and store the…
articles.body: Implement File Export with Temporary Download Links Using Presigned URLs Short answer: keep the exported file private, generate a presigned download link only after the export completes, and store the retention deadline separately so deletion remains testable. A presigned URL is the right delivery primitive for an exported training artifact when the link should expire and the storage bucket should stay private. The important design decision comes before the link: define the artifact's retention class, record the deletion deadline beside the export, and make the export job reproducible enough that a retry cannot quietly create a second copy.

articles.body: When you use a general-purpose LLM to analyze a stock or read an earnings report, it tends to agree with whatever premise you put in the prompt. If you ask why a company looks undervalued, it will assemble a convincing bull case. In financial research, that habit is risky. I built DisconfirmAI around a simple rule from Karl Popper and value investing: before building conviction in a thesis, look for the specific evidence that would prove it wrong. articles.body: I'm the developer of MakeQuickWork, a small collection of free browser tools. This post is about how one of them, PDF to JPG, works under the hood. Most "PDF to JPG" sites follow the same pattern: you upload the file, a server renders it, and you download a ZIP a few seconds later. That works, but it means a contract, a payslip or a medical letter sits on someone else's server for a while. I wanted a version where the PDF never leaves the browser tab. It turned out to be a nice little exercise in canvas, DPI math and browser quirks. The tool is live at https://makequickwork.com/pdf/pdf-to-jpg/ if you want to follow along with DevTools open. The pipeline The whole thing is four steps, all client side: Read the File the user picked into an ArrayBuffer .

articles.title: AI Agents Have the Keys to Your Computer. I Spent 8 Months Building an Antivirus for Them.
articles.excerpt: A coding agent with terminal access can install a package, run a script, start a child process and connect to a server. Add skills, hooks and MCP tools, and a request like “fix the build” can become a…
articles.body: A coding agent with terminal access can install a package, run a script, start a child process and connect to a server. Add skills, hooks and MCP tools, and a request like “fix the build” can become a chain of actions with access to your files and credentials. Those actions need security decisions. Which command may run? Which tool call did I actually approve? What should happen when an agent touches a sensitive path? I've spent eight months building AEGIS: an open-source security and protection app for local AI agents . “Antivirus for AI agents” is how I describe the project.

articles.body: I can’t remember what I had for lunch yesterday, but I still remember the day Super Mario Sunshine launched in 2002. It was a summer's day and I couldn’t wait to line up at the GameStop in the Natick Mall to pick up my pre-ordered copy. It was getting rave reviews — a 9.4 from IGN, a 9.75 from Game Informer, perfect marks from Nintendo Power! — so it felt like an instant classic. Players at the time seemed to agree, considering that the 3D platformer would go on to become the third best-selling GameCube game of all time. Everyone loved Super Mario Sunshine.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 26, 2004: Cassini spacecraft takes 1st-ever closeup photos of Saturn moon Titan
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. The Cassini spacecraft would later drop off a probe on Titan named Huygens, which was a European spacecraft that hitched a ride to the Saturn system with the Cassini mission. But before Cassini dropped off its robotic passenger, it flew by Titan a few times and took some amazing photos . Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby , and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen.
